implementation_notes: Go initializes package-level variables eagerly, so deferral is written as a value wrapped in a one-time function: `var cfg = sync.OnceValue(loadConfig)` (Go 1.21+) returns a function that runs loadConfig exactly once and returns the same result on every call - the release notes describe this as lazily initializing a value on first use. sync.OnceFunc covers the statement form and sync.OnceValues the (value, error) form. Two Go-specific consequences: the returned function is safe for concurrent use, and failures are cached like successes - a panicking or error-returning first attempt is replayed for every later caller, so an acquisition you may need to retry must not be wrapped in a Once. sync.Once.Do is the pre-1.21 form and behaves identically.
pitfalls: sync.Once caches the outcome: after a panicking first call every later call panics with the same value (the package documents this for OnceFunc, OnceValue and OnceValues), so a transient failure can never be retried through the same Once - use a mutex with a checked state, or singleflight (golang.org/x/sync/singleflight), when retries must be possible.
A lazily acquired value returned as an interface can be a typed nil: returning a nil *T on failure still yields a non-nil interface value, so the error check passes while the caller's methods panic.
sync.Once must not be copied - it embeds a noCopy sentinel - so holding one by value in a struct that gets copied silently breaks the once-only guarantee (go vet reports it).

`var x = sync.OnceValue(f)` runs the declaration at package init but not f: the deferral also hides the acquisition from readers of init(), so call the function explicitly during start-up when the resource is boot-critical.

variants.name: Package var plus sync.Once.Do holder
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-1.21 shape, and still the right one when initialization sets several values, needs parameters, or must keep the acquired handle in its own field: one sync.Once plus the holder variables, with the accessor calling once.Do. Because the closure writes package state, keep the values unexported and return them from the accessor so callers cannot observe a half-initialized holder.
pitfalls: Same cached-outcome rule as OnceValue: the closure never runs again after the first call, so a failed attempt is permanent unless a mutex plus a state check replaces the Once.
The closure captures package state; writing extra fields from outside the closure reintroduces exactly the race the Once removed.
Guard the error as well as the handle: callers that ignore the returned error will use a nil *sql.DB and panic on first query.
